47	Ideally, coalition members collectively identify and implement interventions with previously demonstrated potential to address local priorities effectively (Hawkins et al., 2008). Studies have found sustained improvements in youth outcomes to be associated with coalitions' use of evidence -based practices (EBPs) (Hawkins et al., 2014; Oesterle et al., 2018; Spoth et al., 2022). In practice, however, many coalitions do not select and implement such EBP (Gloppen et al., 2016). The community -based organizations involved in coalitions also often struggle to implement EBPs because of staf fi ng and funding constraints (Bach -Mortensen et al., 2018). Such constraints may also impede inclusive leadership, which requires substantial time, as well as the development of coalition leader skills. The current study focuses on how inclusive leadership, de fi ned as valuing members' distinctive perspectives and fostering a sense of belonging (Shore et al., 2011), affects coalition use of EBPs. Our overarching conceptualization derives from the Community Coalition Action Theory (Kegler & Swan, 2011) and related work by Brown et al. (2016), which draw on prior research and practice to describe how coalition functioning may affect program implementation and hence health outcomes. Key elements of coalition functioning noted in these frameworks include leadership, communication, and decision making, which are expected to affect member engagement, program planning and implementation, and hence community outcomes.
48

(2016) do not provide speci fi c causal logic about how leadership may translate into more or less effective program selection and implementation. To clarify our predictions for the current study, we therefore also draw on the teams literature about how leadership affects decision quality and implementation. This is based on viewing coalitions as teams, that is, interdependent groups of people who communicate over time (Homans, 1958), and the premise that the social dynamics at the heart of teams are potentially applicable across a variety of settings.

The means for inclusive decision making and inclusion of community residents were 4.06 and 4.01 on a 1-5 scale. The number of EBPs reported ranged from 0 to 9. The range of EBP reach was 0 to 5370, but highly skewed, with a mean of 224. The average coalition service area included approximately 84,000 people. The majority of coalitions were in Pennsylvania (86%). Twenty-six (41%) of the 64 coalitions followed the Coalitions That Care model. The majority (64%) reported receiving external funding. Forty-one (64%) of the coalitions received TA. The average coalition size was 36 members. After controlling for covariates and the initial value of each outcome, engaging communication and inclusive decision making showed significant associations (p<.05) with the number of EBPs a year later. Inclusion of community residents was positively associated with number of EBPs, but the association was only marginally significant, at p=.07 (Table 2). Each of these inclusive leadership practices was also shown to have significant positive associations (p<.05 in each case) with the reach of coalitions' evidence-based practices a year later (Table 3). In contrast, none of the inclusive leadership practices that we examined was associated with subsequent EBP fidelity (Table 4). In the fully adjusted lagged models for the number of EBPs and EBP fidelity, none of the covariates remained significant. paper_metadata.authors: Wells, R., Ranjit, N., Brown, L. D., Chilenski, S. M., & Gaddy, Y. M.
paper_metadata.study_design: Lagged observational analysis (1-year lag) of 64 youth substance misuse prevention coalitions in Pennsylvania and Missouri, nested within a randomized technical-assistance trial; Poisson, negative binomial and hierarchical linear regressions. Funded by NIDA R01DA045815.

studies.label: Coalition Check-Up lagged cohort: 64 PA/MO youth substance misuse prevention coalitions, Wave 1 (2020-2021) to Wave 2 (2021-2022)
studies.unit_of_analysis: Coalition for Tables 1-3 (n=64); program nested within coalition for Table 4 (101 programs in 35 coalitions, coalition as random intercept)

hypotheses.statement: Greater engaging communication by coalition leaders at baseline predicts greater coalition use of EBPs one year later (number of EBPs, EBP reach, and EBP fidelity).
hypotheses.provenance_quote: we expected that engaging communication and including both agency representatives and community residents in decision making would improve coalition use of EBPs

hypotheses.statement: Greater inclusive decision making at baseline predicts greater coalition use of EBPs one year later (number, reach, fidelity).
hypotheses.provenance_quote: we expected that engaging communication and including both agency representatives and community residents in decision making would improve coalition use of EBPs

hypotheses.statement: Greater inclusion of community residents at baseline predicts greater coalition use of EBPs one year later (number, reach, fidelity).
hypotheses.provenance_quote: Including local residents in decision making may also improve the use of evidence -based practices.

hypotheses.statement: The three inclusive leadership practices predict EBP implementation fidelity. This prediction was explicitly not supported and is reported as a null result.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: It is not yet clear how inclusive leadership improves evidence -based practice fi delity.

Under the Measures reading, NO coalition can exceed 4, so the proportion above 4 is necessarily 0/64; the tool shows that is very hard to reconcile with mean 3.83 / SD 0.42 (expected 34.3% above 4, binomial p = 3.0e-12). I have DOWNGRADED the tool's own 'highly_suspicious' to 'suspicious' because the test assumes normality, and a ceiling-bounded aggregate would be left-skewed, which weakens (though does not remove) the inference.
